# Daily Papers
The project automatically fetches the latest papers from arXiv based on keywords.

The subheadings in the README file represent the search keywords.

Only the most recent articles for each keyword are retained, up to a maximum of 100 papers.

You can click the 'Watch' button to receive daily email notifications.

Last update: 2026-10-20

| **[Spatial Distribution of Mean PAoI in LEO Satellite-enabled IoT Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23597v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs), such as Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, can provide consistent coverage for Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, particularly in rural areas where cellular coverage is lacking. These IoT nodes are used to monitor and record their surroundings, supporting various applications, including real-time applications. In such cases, transmission of the most up-to-date data is essential, making the Age of Information (AoI) a critical metric to consider. The AoI measures the elapsed time from the data generation at the source node to its reception at the destination. Moreover, the Peak AoI (PAoI), which denotes the maximum AoI in the system before an update is received, provides valuable insights into the network's performance. Therefore, this encourages us to focus on the PAoI within a large-scale and fully loaded IoT network, which is covered by LEOSATs. Using tools from stochastic geometry, this paper derives the spatial distribution of the uplink mean PAoI in a LEOSAT-enabled IoT network. To achieve that purpose, the meta distribution of the uplink conditional coverage probability is derived. Numerical results articulate how varying the number of deployed LEOSATs and their altitudes affects the coverage probability meta distribution and the spatial distribution of the mean PAoI. Additionally, by examining various scenarios with different numbers of LEOSATs and altitudes, we can derive valuable insights to determine the optimal beamwidth for LEOSATs tailored to each specific scenario to minimize the conditional mean PAoI.</p></details> |  |
| **[Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23504v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Weighted spatial averages from incomplete networks are ratios whose variance is approximated by truncating a Taylor series (the delta method). Three questions remain open: whether the series converges, how large a truncation's error is, and how it behaves as the network grows. We address these for observations missing completely at random, independently with a common probability $α$. First, the truncations, which count corrections for the denominator (the total reported weight) and for its coupling with the numerator, converge for a given network only if $α>\tfrac12$ and both corrections increase together. Second, whether or not the series converges, the error of truncations correcting only for the denominator is controlled at any network size by its coefficient of variation $ρ$, with $ρ^2=\tfrac{1-α}α\sum_iβ_i^2$ for weights $β_i$, and by the probability of rare reporting patterns. Third, for uniform weights and bounded fields, these errors vanish as the network grows, at any fixed availability. If correlations also decay with distance, the first-order approximation of earlier work has error of order $ρ^4$, against $ρ^2$ for the simplest approximation. Only truncations of equal order in numerator and denominator, beginning with the first-order truncation, avoid spurious dependence on the mean level; higher ones need not be more accurate. The exact variance for uniform weights, a single sum, shows that for correlated fields the first-order approximation overstates the contribution of missing data but is conservative overall. Concentrated weights degrade it more than $ρ$ indicates. Rainfall simulations over India illustrates results, several of which extend to self-normalized estimators.</p></details> |  |
| **[Scaling Spatially Varying Distributed Lag Nonlinear Models for Nationwide Small-Area Data: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23501v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Lagged and nonlinear exposure-response relationships are frequently modelled using distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs). However, these relationships can vary substantially across locations due to differences in climate, population structure, adaptation and socio-economic characteristics, among others. Spatially-varying DLNMs can capture this heterogeneity, but their computational demands limit their application to fine-scale nationwide datasets with thousands of small areas. In this paper, we adapt a 'divide-and-conquer' approach to spatially varying DLNMs. The method partitions the spatial domain into smaller regions, expands each region with a k-order neighbourhood to reduce boundary effects, fits separate models within each partition using Laplacian P-splines, and combines the resulting estimates using conditional predictive ordinate-based mixture weights. We evaluated the approach in a simulation study based on municipalities in Sicily and applied it to daily summer temperature and mortality data from 7122 municipalities in mainland Italy between 2011 and 2021. Simulation studies show good performance, with relative-risk estimates comparable to those from a global model and relatively robust to the choice and number of partitioning units. Computational efficiency can be substantially improved by using parallel computations. The Italian application reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in the temperature-mortality relationship, with clear regional differences. The proposed framework makes spatially varying DLNMs feasible for large, fine-scale spatiotemporal datasets while retaining location-specific exposure-lag-response estimation.</p></details> |  |
| **[GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23416v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.</p></details> |  |
| **[STC-MGNet: Spatial-Temporal-Channel Attention-Enhanced Multimodal Graph Network for Pedestrian Intention Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23356v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Accurate prediction of pedestrian crossing intentions plays a critical role in enhancing the safety of pedestrian-vehicle interactions in autonomous driving. However, effectively capturing subtle spatiotemporal patterns in pedestrian pose sequences and integrating complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information remain challenging. This paper proposes a spatial-temporal-channel attention-enhanced multimodal graph network (STC-MGNet) for pedestrian crossing intention prediction. STC-MGNet introduces a spatial-temporal-channel (STC) attention-enhanced pose graph encoder to learn discriminative representations from pedestrian pose sequences. Three parallel attention branches selectively emphasize informative skeletal joints, observation frames, and feature channels, with their outputs integrated through learnable fusion weights. To leverage complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information, a multi-stage cross-modal channel modulation mechanism is introduced to adaptively refine pose representations through modality-specific channel gating at successive graph encoding stages. Experimental results demonstrate that STC-MGNet achieves accuracy rates of 70%, 87%, and 88% on the JAADbeh, JAADall, and PIE datasets, respectively, outperforming several representative baseline methods. Ablation experiments further highlight the complementary contributions of visual and ego-vehicle motion information to prediction performance.</p></details> |  |
| **[Look, Reason, Draw a Region: Recursive Refinement for Spatial Context Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23302v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Spatial context prediction requires visual grounding and spatial reasoning to identify vacant regions relative to objects in a scene. Spatial relationships and physical constraints remain challenging for large vision-language models (VLMs). Recursive reasoning has demonstrated strong performance on discrete and abstract reasoning tasks, motivating its use for improving spatial context prediction in natural images. Weight sharing enables higher accuracy with a small trainable parameter count. We introduce Spatial-TRM, a compact recursive model with frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and just 11.2M trainable parameters. This weight-tied reasoner supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On the RoboSpatial-Home benchmark, Spatial-TRM achieves 29.51% context accuracy, a gain of 9.02 percentage points (44.0% relative) over a separately trained single-step model with the same parameter count. Including the frozen encoders, the model has 877.8M total parameters, approximately $15\times$ fewer than the reported 13B size of RoboPoint. These results show that repeated refinement improves spatial context prediction from pretrained vision-language features at a fixed trainable parameter count on this benchmark.</p></details> | <details><summary>17 pa...</summary><p>17 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables</p></details> |
| **[SpaceCast-Bench: Evaluating Predictive Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12402v2)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks mainly test spatial perception: reading off relations already visible in the input. Yet real-world spatial intelligence demands predictive spatial reasoning: constructing a scene from observations, anticipating how an intervention changes it, and reasoning about the unseen outcome. We introduce SpaceCast-Bench, the first benchmark to directly and diagnostically evaluate this capability. Built around an observe-transform-infer framework, its 3,862 questions from 182 real-world scenes span 16 task types at three levels: static perception, local prediction, and global prediction, progressively requiring scene understanding, spatial state updating, and relational inference over unobserved outcomes. Evaluating 21 models exposes a stark gap: the strongest model reaches only 58.0% against 87.2% human performance, while spatially specialized models remain near random chance. Controlled analyses further reveal that bridge views are critical for integrating distributed observations, and that explicit 3D evidence benefits models more reliably than generated outcome images or videos. Fine-tuning on our programmatically generated data lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 34.0% to 65.7% with macro-average gains across six out-of-domain benchmarks.</p></details> | <details><summary>Proje...</summary><p>Project Page: https://zjureal.com/SpaceCast-Bench Code: https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SpaceCast-Bench</p></details> |
| **[Framing Spatial Hearing within the Free Energy Principle: A Hierarchical Model of Perceptual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23196v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Spatial hearing relies on dynamic internal representations to decode spatial information from ever-changing acoustic conditions. A fundamental example is sound localisation, where listeners infer the direction of an invisible sound. Bayesian inference provides a computational account of such a localisation process; however, modelling efforts are largely limited to static listening scenarios. Instead, the free energy principle (FEP) describes perception, learning, and action as joint minimisation of variational free energy (VFE), providing a principled framework to account for dynamic conditions. Here, we take a first step toward applying the FEP to spatial hearing. We characterise how listeners' beliefs evolve across trials, in which they estimated sound direction and received subsequent visual feedback on each trial. Listeners are described by a hierarchical generative model where visual feedback drives gradient descent on VFE, updating beliefs over three independent quantities: lateral and polar localisation precisions and hemifield disambiguation. The model captures individual learning trajectories and reveals components with different dynamics: lateral precision improves, as does hemifield disambiguation, consistent with increased sensitivity of the auditory pathway in decoding vertical direction. Notably, polar precision also increases, most for listeners with the lowest initial precision, suggesting that the observed vertical improvement is driven by both hemifield disambiguation and polar precision. This work establishes spatial hearing as a tractable domain for FEP and motivates future closed-loop experiments with full action-perception cycles.</p></details> |  |
| **[Covert Digital Semantic Communication With Movable Antennas: Constellation Shaping, Spatial Optimization, and Semantic Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23076v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Digital semantic communication (SemCom) is emerging as a bandwidth-efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless networks by delivering the meaning of a source over finite constellations. However, the broadcast nature of wireless channels exposes transmissions to adversarial wardens, while discrete symbols deviate from the Gaussian signaling assumed by conventional covert communication. In this paper, we propose a covert digital SemCom system assisted by movable antennas (MAs), where the constellation, the antenna positions, and the semantic transceiver are jointly designed to conceal the transmission while preserving the semantic fidelity. Specifically, the maximum covert rate against the optimal detector with unknown noise level is derived in closed-form, which reveals that the legitimate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales with the moment-matching order of the constellation and the spatial gain provided by the MA array. A Gauss-Laguerre ring constellation is then designed to raise the moment-matching order under the peak power constraints, and a covert symbol mapping with rank-to-ring assignment and scrambling is developed to carry the semantics in the ordering of the latent magnitudes. Guided by the derived semantic distortion bound, the semantic encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end through an invertible flow over the designed constellation and MA array. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme supports a higher achievable covert rate and improves the reconstruction quality by 24% compared to state-of-the-art SemCom schemes.</p></details> | <details><summary>13 pa...</summary><p>13 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)</p></details> |
| **[PruneGround: Plug-and-play Spatial Pruning for 3D Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31148v3)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) aims to localize target objects in 3D scenes given natural language descriptions. Existing approaches typically perform reasoning over the entire scene, leading to ambiguous predictions and high computational cost, especially in cluttered environments. We observe that many referential expressions rely on local spatial context and often correspond to restricted spatial regions rather than the full scene. Motivated by this insight, we propose PruneGround, an effective plug-and-play framework for 3DVG built upon three key components. First, we introduce Language-Guided Spatial Pruning (LGSP), which leverages a frozen Vision Language Model (VLM) to identify language-relevant regions, thereby reducing spatial computation and grounding candidates in the narrower search space. Second, we propose MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation (MCDR), which decomposes complex expressions into simplified target--anchor relations and augments missing spatial cues through multi-view reasoning. Finally, we propose LLM-Grounder, which repurposes a detection-pretrained spatial LLM into a language-conditioned grounding model by aligning point cloud and linguistic representations within the pruned region. Extensive experiments on the three most popular point cloud benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on all three ScanRefer settings and on 9 out of 10 Nr3D/Sr3D settings. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/PruneGround</p></details> | EMNLP 2026 (Oral) |
| **[Leveraging Cell-level Spatial Transcriptomics as Weak Supervision for Nuclei Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23481v2)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Deep learning-based nuclei analysis in histopathology relies heavily on large-scale, expert-curated datasets that are costly and difficult to scale across organs. Cell-level ST provides both gene expression profiles and nucleus masks, enabling automatic generation of image-label pairs without manual annotation. We convert gene expression into cell-type labels and introduce an image-oriented classification strategy to effectively transfer these identities to histopathology images. Evaluated on unseen tissues, our framework achieves comparable segmentation and classification performance compared with conventional supervised approaches, despite using fewer manually annotated datasets.</p></details> |  |
| **[Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22736v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.</p></details> | <details><summary>Submi...</summary><p>Submiited to ICRA 2027</p></details> |
| **[Same Goal, Different Words: Spatial Instruction Sensitivity in World-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16242v3)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>World-action models should preserve the intended manipulation across equivalent descriptions of a spatial goal. We evaluate this consistency in 864 rollouts from three models across four RoboLab scenes, holding initial states and task goals fixed. Describing relations through the reference object rather than the object-to-move lowers the rate of reaching a stable placement by 12.2 percentage points on average. The effect of instruction rephrasing varies across spatial relations, so aggregate scores can hide sensitivity to wording. Standalone tests of the policies' language understanding identify relation reversals and show that adding images can disrupt otherwise correct text-only interpretations. Rollout analysis also distinguishes spatial placement from instruction following: moving the wrong object can satisfy the requested relation, and rates of stable placement fall from 43.2% at any time to 21.8% at episode end. These findings motivate a more thorough evaluation of world-action models' steerability, language understanding, and grounding. Evaluations should test consistency across equivalent instructions, verify that the intended object moved, and check whether the requested arrangement persists to the end of the rollout.</p></details> | <details><summary>18 pa...</summary><p>18 pages, including appendices. Restored the four-page main-text layout and corrected the General Motors affiliation. Institutional disclaimer retained; scientific content unchanged</p></details> |
| **[Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22700v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.</p></details> |  |
| **[Borrowing Space, Clustering Temporal Dynamics: Bayesian Regime Mapping and Spatial Prediction for European PM10](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22699v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Daily particulate matter measurements from European monitoring networks vary both through spatially shared fluctuations and through differences in local temporal dynamics. Characterising both features is important for identifying groups of monitoring locations with similar temporal behaviour and for predicting concentrations at unmonitored sites. We develop a Bayesian model that combines a continuous spatial common-shock process with a spatial product partition prior for clustering locations according to their local persistence and innovation variability. At unmonitored locations, the model extends these components through spatial interpolation and probabilistic regime allocation. Sparse spatial computations and online prediction summaries make inference feasible for 2,989 monitoring locations and 5,297 unmonitored land locations over 2024. Replicated simulations show that geographic information improves recovery of weakly separated, spatially organised regimes, while uncertainty in regime allocation need not prevent useful continuous prediction. The European analysis identifies stable clusters spanning national boundaries. Clusters with similar persistence nevertheless differ in local innovation variability and in how consistently their stations are grouped together across posterior draws. Comparisons with three restricted models clarify the complementary roles of spatially shared variation, heterogeneous local dynamics and geographic information in the partition.</p></details> |  |
| **[EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22681v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.</p></details> |  |
| **[A Bayesian hierarchical model for preferentially sampled spatial extremes data: an application to air quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22577v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) establish concentration limits for criteria pollutants in order to safeguard public health and the environment. For some NAAQS, the standard refers to thresholds for either high percentiles or maxima. Identifying regions where regulatory thresholds are exceeded involves using geostatistical models, often formulated under the implicit assumption that observations arise from locations randomly sampled in the spatial domain. However, this does not hold for air pollution monitors as they are often preferentially placed in areas with elevated extreme concentration levels. Using the yearly maximum concentration of PM2.5 as a case study, we investigate whether preferential sampling affects inference and prediction for spatial extremes. To this goal, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for preferential sampling by introducing a shared latent, spatial process that informs both the median of the blended Generalized Extreme Value (bGEV) distribution and the probability that a site is selected to be a sampling location. Application of the proposed model to simulated data reveals that, not accounting for preferential sampling, results in systematic biases in parameters estimates, whereas application to observations of yearly maxima PM2.5 concentrations in California between 2017 and 2024 shows that not accounting for preferential sampling can significantly alter conclusions about exceedance regions.</p></details> | 34 pages, 5 figures |
| **[Structure-Aware Spatial Kernels for Gaussian Process Distributed Port-Hamiltonian Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22575v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Gaussian process distributed port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-dPHS) enable data-driven modeling of distributed dynamical systems while preserving their physical structure. This modular construction allows qualitative knowledge of spatial heterogeneity to be incorporated by selecting an appropriate spatial kernel without requiring an analytical description of the underlying profile. Numerical experiments on a nonlinear string with periodic, smoothly varying, and semi-piecewise stiffness profiles demonstrate that structural decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, while profile-matched spatial kernels yield substantially larger gains in force-field and trajectory reconstruction.</p></details> | <details><summary>8 pag...</summary><p>8 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/Wilson-hacker/Softrod_PIML_Project</p></details> |
| **[DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22356v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.</p></details> | <details><summary>Proje...</summary><p>Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/</p></details> |
| **[Spark-0: Scaling Spatially Aligned Tactile Pretraining for Robot Dexterous Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22342v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining. The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.</p></details> | <details><summary>Websi...</summary><p>Website: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0</p></details> |
| **[MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22276v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To address this, we propose CallosumNet, a spatio-temporal graph unlearning framework biologically inspired by the corpus callosum structure. CallosumNet makes two key technical contributions: (1) it reconstructs subgraphs using biologically-inspired virtual edges; and (2) it restores interlinked spatio-temporal dependencies among subgraphs via a lightweight meta-graph integration layer. Empirical results on four diverse real-world datasets show that CallosumNet achieves complete unlearning while maintaining accuracy very close to the gold model. | **[LagNet: Lag-Structured Operators for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23735v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Long-term time series forecasting maps a finite history window to an extended future horizon. Many existing models focus primarily on the design of input representations and model structures, while paying less attention to the structural form of the history-to-future forecasting operator itself. We examine this operator directly and find that, across model families, sensitivity matrices exhibit recurring diagonal patterns whose diagonals correspond to relative temporal lags. Motivated by this observation, we develop a framework for direct multi-step forecasting based on lag-structured temporal operators. Its basic building block, LagLayer, constructs a Toeplitz matrix by tying history-to-future connections with the same relative lag and incorporates horizon-wise and history-wise scaling coefficients to relax exact sharing. This design enables LagLayer to serve as an effective replacement for temporal linear layers in existing forecasting models. Stacking LagLayer modules with activations and multiple feature maps yields LagNet. Experiments on long-term time series forecasting benchmarks show that our method is competitive with strong baselines, while sensitivity matrix diagnostics and limited-data experiments demonstrate that LagLayer provides an effective and sample-efficient alternative to a linear layer.</p></details> |  |

To this end, we introduce RoBERTa-RT, a model trained on human eye-tracking data to predict word-level reading times. We evaluate the model on both internal and external test sets, construct a paired dataset of 496 human-written articles and their LLM-generated rewrites, and apply RoBERTa-RT to compare their predicted reading times. Our findings show that LLM-generated rewrites tend to be shorter and have slightly lower predicted total reading times, while exhibiting higher predicted reading times per word. These differences are associated with systematic linguistic changes, including longer and less frequent words, greater lexical diversity, and higher contextual predictability. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that LLM-generated writing may redistribute reading demands: reducing the amount of text to process while increasing the predicted processing effort associated with individual words. Second, at each temporal operator, the weight of its gradient on the violating samples must stay bounded away from zero, however long the horizon. We introduce lower approximations of the minimum and the maximum whose gradients are sparsemax projections, and we prove that the robustness built from them has both. The gradient of each approximation is exactly zero on every sample beyond a data-dependent threshold, so the weight on violating samples a gap beyond the others has a positive lower bound at every horizon. | **[Optimizing Singular Spectrum for Large Language Model Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15092v2)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet prohibitive parameter complexity often hinders their deployment. Existing singular value decomposition (SVD) based compression methods simply deem singular values as importance scores of decomposed components. However, this importance ordered by singular values does not necessarily correlate with the performance of a downstream task. In this work, we introduce SoCo (Singular spectrum optimization for large language model Compression), a novel compression framework that learns to rescale the decomposed components of SVD in a data-driven manner. Concretely, we employ a learnable diagonal matrix to assign importance scores for singular spectrum and develop a three-stage training process that progressively refines these scores from initial coarse compression to fine-grained sparsification-thereby striking an effective balance between aggressive model compression and performance preservation. Thanks to the learnable singular spectrum, SoCo adaptively prunes components according to the sparsified importance scores, rather than relying on the fixed order of singular values. More importantly, the remaining components with amplified importance scores can compensate for the loss of the pruned ones. Experimental evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that SoCo surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in model compression.</p></details> |  |

To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. Existing algorithms for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings are either slow for short strings or require quadratic time and fail to scale to long strings. To reduce the number of string comparisons, state-of-the-art techniques perform an index-nested-loop join on trie-based indexes; however, they have only been evaluated on small datasets and high similarity thresholds. (2) Dual-bound intersection bitmaps encode strings -- represented as character sets -- into fixed-size bitmaps, which are used to prune candidate string pairs by providing effective bounds on their character overlap; unlike prior bitmap techniques, our bitmaps are equipped with a cost model and adapt to the input data. | **[Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15029v1)** | 2026-10-10 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.</p></details> |  |
| **[Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14998v1)** | 2026-10-10 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.</p></details> |  |
| **[D$^{2}$-VPR: A Parameter-efficient Visual-foundation-model-based Visual Place Recognition Method via Knowledge Distillation and Deformable Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12528v5)** | 2026-10-10 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Visual Place Recognition (VPR) aims to determine the geographic location of a query image by retrieving its most visually similar counterpart from a geo-tagged reference database. Recently, the emergence of the powerful visual foundation model, DINOv2, trained in a self-supervised manner on massive datasets, has significantly improved VPR performance. This improvement stems from DINOv2's exceptional feature generalization capabilities but is often accompanied by increased model complexity and computational overhead that impede deployment on resource-constrained devices. To address this challenge, we propose $D^{2}$-VPR, a $D$istillation- and $D$eformable-based framework that retains the strong feature extraction capabilities of visual foundation models while significantly reducing model parameters and achieving a more favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. Specifically, first, we employ a two-stage training strategy that integrates knowledge distillation and fine-tuning. Additionally, we introduce a Distillation Recovery Module (DRM) to better align the feature spaces between the teacher and student models, thereby minimizing knowledge transfer losses to the greatest extent possible. Second, we design a Top-Down-attention-based Deformable Aggregator (TDDA) that leverages global semantic features to dynamically and adaptively adjust the Regions of Interest (ROI) used for aggregation, thereby improving adaptability to irregular structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Meanwhile, it reduces the parameter count by approximately 64.2% (compared to CricaVPR).Code is available at https://github.com/tony19980810/D2VPR.</p></details> |  |
| **[GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14541v1)** | 2026-10-10 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.</p></details> | <details><summary>22 pa...</summary><p>22 pages. Project page: https://duangzhu.github.io/GG-Nav-Project-Page/</p></details> |
| **[DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14497v1)** | 2026-10-10 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accep...</summary><p>Accepted at NeurIPS 2026</p></details> |
| **[DexFLEX: Contact-Aware Foundation Controller for Command-Guided Dexterity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14372v1)** | 2026-10-09 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.</p></details> |  |
